title: Put the five steps of risk assessment in order
prompt: Drag (or tap) each step into the order the book gives.
items: Identify the hazards
Decide who might be harmed and how
Evaluate the risks and decide on precautions
Record the findings and put them into practice
Review the assessment regularly, updating it when conditions change
quotes: HSE sets out five steps for carrying one out properly: identify the hazards; decide who might be harmed and how; evaluate the risks and decide on precautions; record the findings and put them into practice; and review the assessment regularly, updating it when conditions change.
The five steps are tested in order more often than you'd expect: Identify, Decide who's harmed, Evaluate and decide precautions, Record and implement, Review.

title: Put the hierarchy of control in order
prompt: Drag (or tap) each step into the right order, most effective first.
items: Eliminate the hazard
Substitute it with something less hazardous
Engineering controls (e.g. guardrails, barriers, extraction)
Administrative controls (e.g. training, signage, procedures, permits)
Personal protective equipment (PPE)
quotes: the hierarchy of control sets out the order in which control measures should be considered, from most to least effective: eliminate the hazard entirely wherever possible; substitute it with something less hazardous if elimination isn't possible;

use engineering controls — physical measures such as guardrails, barriers, or extraction systems — to isolate people from the hazard; apply administrative controls such as training, signage, procedures, and permits to work;
and only then rely on personal protective equipment (PPE) as the last line of defence.
E-S-E-C-P: Eliminate, Substitute, Engineering, Control (admin), PPE — from most to least effective.

title: Put the Work at Height hierarchy in order
prompt: Drag (or tap) each level into the order it must be worked through, first consideration first.
items: Avoid working at height altogether (e.g. do the task from ground level)
Prevent a fall (safe place of work or collective protection such as guardrails)
Minimise the distance and consequences of a fall (nets or soft-landing systems, then a harness)
quotes: The Work at Height Regulations 2005 set out a strict three-level hierarchy that must be worked through in order, not chosen freely.
First, avoid working at height altogether wherever it's reasonably practicable — doing a task from ground level instead.
Second, where it can't be avoided, prevent a fall from happening, using an existing safe place of work or collective protection such as guardrails before any personal equipment.
Third, where a fall still can't be ruled out, minimise its distance and consequences, using nets or soft-landing systems before a personal fall arrest harness as the last resort.
The hierarchy is strict and sequential — avoid, then prevent, then minimise.

title: Put the waste hierarchy in order
prompt: Drag (or tap) each option into order, most preferred first.
items: Prevent or reduce waste
Prepare items for reuse
Recycle or compost
Recover energy from waste
Dispose (typically landfill)
quotes: from most to least preferred: preventing or reducing waste in the first place, preparing items for reuse, recycling or composting, recovering energy from waste that can't be reused or recycled, and disposal — typically landfill — as the last resort.
Prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose — in that order, every time.

title: Put the fire evacuation steps in order
prompt: Drag (or tap) each step into the order the book gives.
items: Alarm sounds: stop work immediately and put tools down
Go via the nearest safe, marked route to the designated assembly point
Supervisor or fire marshal carries out a head count against sign-in records
Re-enter only once officially cleared by the emergency services or site management
quotes: When the alarm sounds, work stops immediately — tools are put down, tasks are left unfinished, and everyone proceeds via the nearest safe, marked route to the site's designated assembly point.
At the assembly point, a supervisor or fire marshal carries out a head count against sign-in records, which is how the site confirms whether anyone is still inside and needs rescue.
No one re-enters the site until officially cleared by the emergency services or site management.
Alarm sounds, tools down, straight to the assembly point — no exceptions, no detours.

title: Stop a ladder slipping: order of preference
prompt: Drag (or tap) each method into the book's order of preference, most preferred first.
items: Tie both stiles to a secure point
Use a proprietary stability device
Wedge the base
Foot the ladder with another person (last resort)
quotes: A ladder must also be prevented from slipping, and the methods are used in a strict order of preference: tying both stiles to a secure point, using a proprietary stability device, wedging the base, and only footing the ladder with another person as a last resort when nothing else is practical.

title: Match the HSE enforcement power to what it does
prompt: Drag (or tap) each item on the left onto its matching description.

pairs.right: Gives a set period of time to fix the problem
Stops a dangerous activity immediately
Can follow serious or repeated breaches, with no upper limit on the fine

quotes: they can issue an Improvement Notice, which gives a set period to fix a problem, or a Prohibition Notice, which stops a dangerous activity immediately.
Serious or repeated breaches can lead to prosecution, with no upper limit on the fine a court can impose.
Answer: An Improvement Notice allows a set period of time to fix the problem; a Prohibition Notice stops the dangerous activity immediately.

title: Match the CDM 2015 duty holder to their role
prompt: Drag (or tap) each item on the left onto its matching description.

pairs.right: Commissions the work and must ensure suitable arrangements are in place
Manages health and safety during the pre-construction (design) phase
Takes over health and safety once construction begins; required when more than one contractor is involved
Manage the risks created by their own work

quotes: The Client commissions the work and must ensure suitable arrangements are in place.
The Principal Designer manages health and safety during the pre-construction (design) phase.
The Principal Contractor takes over responsibility for health and safety once construction begins, and is required whenever more than one contractor is involved on a project
Individual contractors remain responsible for managing the risks created by their own work.

title: Match the RIDDOR category to its description
prompt: Drag (or tap) each item on the left onto its matching description.

pairs.right: e.g. a fracture (not fingers, thumbs or toes) or amputation: report without delay, written report within 10 days
Worker unable to do normal duties for more than 7 consecutive days: report within 15 days
A specified near-miss event, such as a scaffold collapse: report without delay
Reported without delay once diagnosis is confirmed

quotes: Deaths and specified injuries — including fractures other than to fingers, thumbs, or toes, amputations, permanent loss of sight, and any injury requiring more than 24 hours in hospital — must be reported without delay, followed by a written report within 10 days.
Injuries that leave a worker unable to carry out their normal duties for more than 7 consecutive days must be reported within 15 days of the accident.

Dangerous occurrences — near-miss events specified in the regulations, such as a scaffold collapse — are also reported without delay, and diagnosed occupational diseases are reported without delay once diagnosis is confirmed.
